title: The seminaries
hookLine: the great seminaries of Najaf and Qom

cards: Morning, in a narrow lane near a golden dome. Two students sit on a mat with one book open between them. One reads a line and explains it.
The other objects. The first pushes back, finds the line again, reads it more slowly. Nobody is angry.
This is the work. Yesterday's marja' doesn't appear out of nowhere. He is made, over long years, in lanes and rooms like this one.
Today, the places that make them.

teach.b: The word is hawzah, the Shia seminary; in full, al-hawzah al-'ilmiyyah, the seat of learning.

teach.h: NAJAF AND QOM, TWO SHRINE CITIES.
teach.b: Today's two cities are Najaf and Qom. Najaf, in Iraq, is the city of the shrine of Imam 'Ali. Tradition says its hawzah grew around the scholar Shaykh al-Tusi, who settled there after leaving Baghdad.
Qom, in Iran, holds the shrine of Fatimah al-Ma'sumah, sister of Imam al-Rida, and its hawzah was revived in modern times. Both are shrine cities; the study happens in the shadow of the domes.
It runs in stages, not fixed years.
First the preliminaries: Arabic grammar, logic, rhetoric. Then the surfaces, the sutuh: set textbooks of law and its method, read line by line with a teacher.

Then the highest stage, bahth al-kharij, study outside the text: a senior teacher lectures on a question with no set book, weighing the evidence and earlier opinions aloud, and students are expected to argue back.
Between lessons, students review in pairs, like the two on the mat. A student chooses teachers, sits in their circles, moves on when ready. Out of long years of that comes a mujtahid.

teach.h: FROM STUDENT TO MUJTAHID TO MARJA'.
teach.b: And from among the mujtahids, through the regard of other scholars and the trust of believers, a marja'. Scholars move between the two cities; a student may begin in one and finish in the other.
In this telling, Najaf and Qom aren't rivals. They're two lamps in the same tradition, on either side of a border.

how: Shia students study at the seminaries of Najaf, Qom and elsewhere, moving from Arabic and logic through set textbooks to advanced lectures beyond the textbook, often reviewing in pairs.

games.q: you're a hawzah student. your study partner reads a line and draws a conclusion you think is wrong. what do you do?
o: object, and argue it out over the book.
games.why: you object. reading in pairs, explaining and pushing back, is part of how the hawzah studies.

practice: On a map or in your mind, find Baghdad and follow south to Najaf, and notice the town beside it: Kufa, Abu Hanifa's city, two schools as close neighbors.
Then cross east into Iran and find Qom, south of Tehran, resting a few breaths on each city.
Last, think of one place where you were really taught something, a classroom, a kitchen, a garage, and if you pray, you can remember your teachers.

wordCard.voice: Hawzah. The Shia seminary, the seat of learning, with its great centers in Najaf and Qom. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: najaf and qom. A scholar is made over long years of reading and arguing. Twelve hundred days, and thank you for each one.
